Day 76 of 100 · Kubernetes

Kubernetes Namespaces

#100DaysOfCloudAndSecurityKubernetesPublished journey entry

Namespaces scope namespaced Kubernetes objects so environments and teams can organize resources without making object names globally unique across the cluster.

Architecture / mental model

cluster → namespace dev / namespace prod → namespaced workloads/services/config

How it works

The same resource name can exist in different namespaces because namespaced API objects are addressed within that scope.

Commands can target a namespace explicitly with `-n`, or the current kubectl context can set a default namespace for convenience.

Namespaces are organizational and policy scopes, not automatic security isolation. RBAC, NetworkPolicy, quotas and admission controls determine what isolation actually exists.

Hands-on reference

kubectl create namespace dev
kubectl create namespace prod
kubectl run web --image=nginx:alpine -n dev
kubectl run web --image=nginx:alpine -n prod
kubectl get pods -n dev
kubectl get pods -n prod
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=dev

Verification

Create identically named disposable objects in two namespaces and prove queries/actions stay scoped. Then inspect RBAC/network policy separately rather than assuming namespace boundaries block access.

Field note / gotcha

Deleting a namespace deletes the namespaced resources inside it. A tidy scope can become a very efficient deletion boundary.

Security considerations

Use namespace-scoped RBAC, resource quotas and network policies where appropriate; do not market namespaces alone as tenant isolation.

What I learned

Namespacing organizes the API. Security comes from the controls applied to that scope.
